🐛 Describe the bug
Doing a research for this issue #72368 I found that  we run sharding algorithm for each of the shard separately. We retreive same data and run same commit then based on the number of current shard and total shard we assign the worker with the test jobs to execute.
The algorithm retrieves a commit from day ago here:
get_previous_reports_for_branch
Issue with this approach, since there are multiple workers its possible that they retrieve different commits (if commits are made within seconds interval) and hence sharding breakdown will be different for different workers, and we will end up with situation where some tests are not executed at all and some tests are executed multiple times.
Proposed solution 1:
Run all sharding algorithm after build have been completed and pass list of jobs to each of the workers
Proposed solution 2:
Reuse same logic but retrieve the day ago commit SHA after build have been completed, then pass SHA to each of the workers and let the workers run sharding algorithm and assign the shards to themselves.

Torch.package  is a handy tool to serialize and deserialize python code. It works as you expect a packager to but with the added benefit of also saving the actual code itself when desired. It was primarily designed with the intention of being the delivery mechanism for torch::deploy which is a runtime for getting pytorch models to run on multiple threads in eager mode. There's a great whitepaper about torch.package and torch::deploy here.
Motivation: There are a decent amount of really annoying pain points for users. One of them is that torch.package is used with a pile of really complicated projects inside Meta (ping me if you're curious which), and eventually outside. These projects have piles on piles of dependencies to manage, and while the API of torch.package gives users really fine grained control, it can be cumbersome. In the case of C++ dependencies, these must be externed as we do not support interning them yet. Therefore, the goal of this task is to add a small feature to automatically extern these dependencies rather than copying over the code.
Currently, what we do is collect the C extension modules and report them as an error in torch/package/PackageExporter. What do this by checking if a module has a C extension in the _intern_module function and then add it to the list of errors we report at the end. We want to replace this behavior with an automatic extern.

Create an optional flag auto_extern_c_extension_modules in the constructor of the PackageExporter. By default it should be False.
If the flag is set to False, things should work as they currently do.
If the flag is set to True, add the module's name to the extern list by using self.extern(...)

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Context:
PostLocalSGDOptimizer can have a non-trivial warm-up stage. E.g., a training may take 30 epochs, and the warmup stage may take 3-5 epochs.
Issue:
If the training process is not very reliable and may fail a few times, then the training needs to resume from checkpoints. However, in the current setup the built-in step counter in ModelAverager will be reset after each restart. As a result, the warm-up stage will run multiple times, which will lead to less speedup.
Proposed Solution:
To be able to skip the warm-up stage after resuming from a checkpiont, the step # across epochs must recorded and stored in the checkpoint as well. A good option is the optimizer state.
Alternatives
If PyTorch Ignite or PyTorch Lightning is used, the global step # will be automatically stored in the checkpoint, and such feature can also be easily supported by modifying the application code.
However, it will be nice to support this feature in PyTorch directly, especially if an optimizer state is already available in this case.

🐛 Describe the bug
When given fp16 inputs and a concentrated index tensor (with repeating indices), the scatter_add function becomes very slow. This does not happen for fp32 inputs.

Below is a minimal code sample to reproduce the problem by plotting the slow down as the index tensor becomes more concentrated:
import torch
import time
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

batch_size = 100
tgt_dim = 1000000
src_dim = 300000
max_spread_pow = 10
fp32_results = []
fp16_results = []

for spread_pow in range(1, max_spread_pow):
    for precision in ["fp32", "fp16"]:
        dtype = torch.float32 if precision == "fp32" else torch.float16
        tgt = torch.zeros(batch_size, tgt_dim).to(dtype).cuda()
        src = torch.rand(batch_size, src_dim).to(dtype).cuda()
        spread = 0.5 ** spread_pow
        index = torch.randint(
            int(tgt_dim / 2 - tgt_dim * spread),
            int(tgt_dim / 2 + tgt_dim * spread),
            (batch_size, src_dim)

            t0 = time.time()
            tgt.scatter_add_(1, index, src)
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            t1 = time.time()

We are making some changes to the implementation of the PyTorch OSS CI so that it’s easier to use, more understandable, and more maintainable. Here is a list of changes, from most general to most power-user-specific.
All pull request CI runs in a single workflow. This makes it easier to see results in the default PR checks view, and (with recent improvements on the GitHub side) means you can rerun all failed PR CI jobs with one click! We are truly the pinnacle of modern technology.
CIFlow tags have been simplified. We had many tags with overlapping coverage that needed to be manually maintained. In practice, people rarely used the “topic” labels and opted to just run everything (e.g. ciflow/all). Now, the tags map directly onto workflows. Want to run all of trunk CI? Use the ciflow/trunk label. Want to run nightlies? Use the ciflow/nightly label, etc. Our bot will tell you if you are using a defunct label.
Codegen has been eliminated, making the CI easier to understand. The previous codegen system evolved piecemeal over time and became somewhat Lovecraftian. After eliminating codegen, it is much easier to understand what runs on pull request vs. trunk, and what test configurations are actually being run.
For technical details of the actual changes, see: https://fb.quip.com/RcLZAOb9k0qI (or ping me if you care and are not a Meta employee)

🐛 Describe the bug
Hello, I recently came across a weird phenomenon when using torch.sign() in my loss function. Specifically, in the calculation of the loss function for a given vector v, I am calculating matrices of the form S_ij = v_i - v_j. In the code below, I made 2 versions of the loss function, and the only difference is:
S_diff = torch.sign((labels[None, :] - labels[:, None]).squeeze().T)
S_diff = torch.sign((labels[:, None] - labels[None, :]).squeeze())
However, the two should be the same, as the transpose takes care of the different ordering between them. Below, I provide a small working example where I include both versions of the loss function, a toy neural network model and then for two equal networks I print the gradients of the final linear layer. What you can observe is that the gradients are not the same. I am unsure what is causing this issue. Although the difference might seem small, the trained models actually give very different final states (as if the one that uses the transpose doesn't learn well). Thank you in advance!
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import copy

# Loss version 1
def compute_lambda_i_version1(scores, labels):
    scores = scores.squeeze(1)
    z_diff = (scores[:, None] - scores[None, :]).squeeze()
    S_diff = torch.sign((labels[None, :] - labels[:, None]).squeeze().T) # Difference

    lambda_i =  (1 - S_diff)  / 2 - 1 /(1 + torch.exp(z_diff))
    lambda_i = lambda_i.sum(axis=1).unsqueeze(1)
        
    return lambda_i 

# Loss version 2
def compute_lambda_i_version2(scores, labels):
    scores = scores.squeeze(1)
    z_diff = (scores[:, None] - scores[None, :]).squeeze()
    S_diff = torch.sign((labels[:, None] - labels[None, :]).squeeze()) # Difference

    lambda_i =  (1 - S_diff)  / 2 - 1 /(1 + torch.exp(z_diff))

    lambda_i = lambda_i.sum(axis=1).unsqueeze(1)
        
    return lambda_i 

# Generic neural net
class NeuralModule(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.network = nn.Sequential(
                        nn.Linear(501,256),
                        nn.ReLU(),
                        nn.Linear(256,1)
                        )
    
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.network(x)
        return x

# Random input
inputs = torch.rand(5, 501)
labels = torch.FloatTensor([1, 2, 3, 0, 4])

# Init the networks
net_1 = NeuralModule()
net_2 = NeuralModule()
net_2.load_state_dict(copy.deepcopy(net_1.state_dict()))

# Network 1 gradients / loss version 1
scores_1 = net_1(inputs)
loss_1 = compute_lambda_i_version1(scores_1, labels)
torch.autograd.backward(scores_1, loss_1)
grad_1 = net_1.network[2].weight.grad

# Network 2 gradients / loss version 2
scores_2 = net_2(inputs)
loss_2 = compute_lambda_i_version2(scores_2, labels)
torch.autograd.backward(scores_2, loss_2)
grad_2 = net_2.network[2].weight.grad

print(torch.equal(grad_1, grad_2))
print(torch.abs(grad_1-grad_2).mean())

🐛 Describe the bug
There is now a major performance regression (1.5X to 4X slower per training iteration) in PyTorch XLA and a minor regression on CUDA after loading optimizer state dict in AdamW and many other optimizers. It happens in the latest master branch on 03/18/2022 (commit c064ea07f6263090a40b1a6fc5fe5973a76785e5).
This is caused by the functional change in optimizers (#71333), which changes state['step'] from int to torch.Tensor and causes state['step'] to be pushed to the same device as the parameter upon load_state_dict.
Taking AdamW as an example, the error is that

state['step'] is originally initialized as a CPU tensor in 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/optim/adamw.py
    
    
         Line 136
      in
      c064ea0
    
  
  
    

        
          
           state['step'] = torch.tensor(0.) 
        
    
  


but in load_state_dict, all the state tensors (including state['step'], state['exp_avg'], and state['exp_avg_sq']) will be cast to the same device as the parameter in 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/optim/optimizer.py
    
    
         Line 177
      in
      c064ea0
    
  
  
    

        
          
           state[param] = cast(param, v) 
        
    
  


this causes state['step'] to be no longer on CPUs after load_state_dict, and now it will be a CUDA tensor or an XLA tensor if the parameter is on CUDA or XLA
in each training iteration, now state['step'] needs to be move back to CPU from CUDA or XLA to compute things like step = step_t.item() in 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/optim/adamw.py
    
    
         Line 245
      in
      c064ea0
    
  
  
    

        
          
           step = step_t.item() 
        
    
  

 or bias_correction1 = [1 - beta1 ** step.item() for step in state_steps] in 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/optim/adamw.py
    
    
         Line 296
      in
      c064ea0
    
  
  
    

        
          
           bias_correction1 = [1 - beta1 ** step.item() for step in state_steps] 
        
    
  


the overhead is especially great in PyTorch XLA since step_t.item() cuts the XLA graph and forces an execution; it also causes a (less severe) performance regression on CUDA due to moving tensors back to CPU

Potential fix:

one should avoid casting state['step'] to CUDA or XLA in load_state_dict and keep it on CPU
another (less ideal) fix would be to cast state['step'] back to CPU somewhere after load_state_dict

Currently, something like this:
for _ in range(100):
    with torchdynamo.optimize(...)
        foo(random.random())

Will cause problems because torchdynamo will specialize on the exact value from random.random(), resulting in guards failing and hitting cache_size_limit quickly.  Another example of this issue is something like a counter, which monotonically increases.
We should add support for not specializing on a Python int/float, and instead passing it as an input into the graph.  An earlier version of TorchDynamo actually did this, but I removed bit because backends had poor support for Python types, so it caused downstream issues.  To do this in a compatible way, we may need to wrap these values in 1-element Tensors before handing them to the backend.
The tricky part seems to be coming up with a good heuristic to decide when to specialize and when not to.  A few thoughts of the inputs to this heuristic:

Use the variable source: if something is a code constant, we know for sure the value is fixed.  Similarly, if something as an attribute of a nn.Module or a global it is also usually fixed.  If something is a default arg (def foo(x, alpha=0.0)) it may also be fixed.  If it is the return value of random.random(), it likely isn't.
Use the value itself: values like 0, 1, 0.5, math.pi all might be good to specialize on, while a less common value might be not be.
Use the usages of the value: if a value goes into control flow, it may be better to specialize on it for bigger graphs.
Use prior guard failures: if we have failed guards on a value changing, the next graph compile to decide to do less specialization and back-off.

All of these seem reasonable.  I might start with a mix of 1/2, as they seem the easiest to implement, but it would be a good thing to iterate on.  If it doubt, we should default to not-specializing.

🐛 Describe the bug
The TL;DR is that
Tensor[int] * ScalarTensor[float64] => Tensor[float64]

but
Tensor[int] * 2.0 => Tensor[float32]

The bug crops up in __torch_dispatch__, where when dispatching for * for something like torch.randint(10, (2,2)) * 2.0 you get args with types Tensor[int], ScalarTensor[float64] and thus you end up having to return Tensor[float64], whereas aten (i.e., vanilla PyTorch) will return Tensor[float32]. This is a problem for compiler backends that want to hook in through __torch_dispatch__ (such as torch-mlir), since the compiler's type promotion semantics will disagree with PyTorch's. A straightforward repro of this using functorch is
import torch
import torch.fx as fx
from functorch.compile import aot_module

def do_nothing_compiler():
    def f(fx_g: fx.GraphModule, inps):
        if hasattr(fx_g, "_tensor_constant0"):
            print(fx_g._tensor_constant0.dtype)
        return fx_g

    return f

class ElementwiseMulScalarModule(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def forward(self, x):
        return torch.mul(x, 8.0)

t = torch.ones((1, 3, 32, 32), dtype=torch.int32)
fn = aot_module(ElementwiseMulScalarModule(), do_nothing_compiler(), do_nothing_compiler())
y = fn(t)
print(y.dtype)
>>> torch.float64 # <---------- dtype that do_nothing_compiler sees for the scalar 8.0
>>> torch.float32 # <---------- dtype that PyTorch returns
I think this is related to wrapped_number and type promotion but I could be wrong.

Debug printouts via the:

print() builtin function
logging builtin library
warnings builtin library
Third party logging/stats libraries

Are all somewhat common in PyTorch code.  Currently, all of these will trigger graph breaks in TorchDynamo.  I have argued breaking the graph on prints is the only correct behavior.  If the user writes:
x = torch.sin(x)
print(time.time())
x = torch.sin(x)
x = torch.sin(x)
print(time.time())
x = torch.sin(x)

Implicitly moving prints to either the start or end of the function may be confusing for users and is not something we should do by default.
That said, I could see the value in adding a reorder_prints=True configuration option to TorchDynamo which would defer all prints to the after the graph.  This would allow larger graphs, with only a small change in program semantics.  It would be easy to implement and add value to users, so we should add it.
The warnings module might be fine to reorder by default.  For third party logging libraries, we might need a system for users register things it is safe to reorder with respect to PyTorch ops.

One idea that I have discussed with a few people and wanted to document here is having the core of PyTorch cooperate with TorchDynamo to reduce the need for guards.
Many of the guards TorchDynamo generates are checking attributes of a tree of nn.Module() objects.
Currently, there are two modes, controlled by the guard_nn_modules flag:
https://github.com/facebookresearch/torchdynamo/blob/0b1e34d53f53937b3066e61a14d210365a24b156/torchdynamo/config.py#L36
With guard_nn_modules=True, dynamo will check the entire nn.Module() tree. With guard_nn_modules=False, dynamo will just check the root id() of the module and assume the module structure is fixed per-instance.  guard_nn_modules=False matches the level of checking TorchScript does, while guard_nn_modules=True is a higher level of correctness guarantee.
A better way to handle this, might be to add a new on_modified() callback/hook to nn.Module.  This would be called whenever:

eval/training mode changes
a parameter changes
a buffer changes
a child module changes
a nn.Module().attr changes (custom attrs, not params/buffers/modules)
If a parameter/buffer's shape/requires_grad/etc are modified in-place (this should only check Tensor metadata, not the values)

These should all be checkable in existing places like __setattr__.  There are a few places that would be hard to catch, and the callback would not be called:

If a python structure (like a list/dict/non-nn.Module object/etc) stored on an nn.Module is mutated.  TorchDynamo can still emit guards for these.

An open question is if this should be a global hook or a per-instance hook.  Per-instance might be more flexible, while global one would be faster since there will be one call rather than many.  (O(n) versus O(n^2) issue in number of GuardedCode()/nn.Module() instances.)
This on_modified hook would allow TorchDynamo to replace guards (which must be checked on the critical path on every call) with a call to GuardedCode.invalidate(), which would have zero overhead on the critical path, but add some overhead when users mutate nn.Module attributes.
TorchDynamo has something similar with the MutationTracker class, which monkey patches user objects to get callbacks to invalidate code.  Note that currently isn't used by default.

Many more of these backends may not be useful, in that they don't provide a performance advantage compared to the other choices or are alternate versions of another backend.  We should do some benchmarking to find these cases and do pruning.
Additionally, many backends require multiple external dependencies to work properly.  We should document what those are and provide instructions on how to set each one up.
I'd propose splitting our set of backends into an external/stable set and an internal/experimental set.  torchdynamo.list_backends() would only include the stable set, while torchdynamo.list_backends(experimental=True) would include the larger set of backends.
All backends in the stable set should have documentation explaining what they are, and instructions on how to install the needed dependencies to get them working.

Perhaps this is a false alarm?  The guard is the same all 3 times which is strange, so perhaps we are generating an incorrect guard?
Perhaps we are over guarding here?  "self.outputs" seems like something we write to, and TorchDynamo thinks it should be empty, so perhaps we actually don't need to guard on it at all
Perhaps there is real mutation in which case we can use convert_to_unspecialized.  There are actually two ways of handling nn.Module in dynamo (specialized and unspecialized). Currently, GuardedCode.invalidate() just sets a flag causing guard checks to always fail.
https://github.com/facebookresearch/torchdynamo/blob/055396468d1cea35cfae8955e59d29299290d592/torchdynamo/guards.py#L364
GuardedCode.invalidate() is called by weakref when something we guarded on is destructed.
This means the memory and compiled artifacts are not freed until one calls torchdynamo.reset().
This could be a problem if the compiled artifacts hold pointers to tensors, and could cause a memory leak.
Ideally we would have some sort of garbage collection where we walk code cache and remove anything that has been invalidated.
We should also do some testing to ensure TorchDynamo is not holding pointers to things and preventing memory from being freed.

nodes.bodyText:
Currently, multiple compiled versions of a code object are stored in a linked list and guards are checked in a reverse order of creation.  One-by-one.
This, requires O(n) guard checks, though we cap it to 64.
In the common case, there is just one compiled version of each code object.  Thus, this data structure is actually very good because it has low overhead and constant factors.
In the case of a single code object with extremely high fan out, this strategy will break down.  A hash table version the code cache could be O(1) and allow us to remove the cache_size_limit.  We could also allow reuse of common guard checks across different compiled versions of a function. We should enable this alternate structure whenever the cache grows past a threshold.
One challenge of this is guards are primarily implemented in python, however the critical parts (like tensor checking) is done in C++.  Since the code cache is on the critical path, it likely needs to be in C/C++.

User impact
How does this affect users of PyTorch CI?
Many jobs on the PRs failed due to a missing file in the Upload stats step, and none of it was the PR author's fault.
Root cause
What was the root cause of this issue?
Because we use the workflow files from the merge of PR head + master but then check out the PR head SHA, this can cause incompatibility for PRs not yet rebased past a workflows change.
In this case, Michael's PR introduced a new file for the upload stats step, but the file was not found for the checked out pytorch/pytorch since we are checking out the PR head which may be before the change.
Mitigation
How did we mitigate the issue?
We didn't, but as time passed, people were not at that awkward in between moment of conflict anymore.
Prevention/followups
How do we prevent issues like this in the future?

Switch back to checking out trunk?
Tell people ahead of time when making a CI change to rebase past the change to not have issues.

PyTorch has many hooks, for example those on nn.Module(), Tensors, and a few stored in global scope.
Currently, TorchDynamo will ignore these hooks and not properly call them.
We should check for hooks, inline them if they exist, and guard on them not changing.
To make the guards cheaper, we could add a "hooks changed" callback to PyTorch, allowing us to invalidate generated code rather than adding guards.
